title: The Spiral, the Collisions, and the Primes

chapters.title: The Stage
chapters.subtitle: A floor, a pole, and a dial

lines.text: Start with an empty stage. A flat floor, and a pole going straight up.
Every point on the floor is a complex number: so many steps to the right, so many steps toward the back.
The pole is a dial. We will turn it slowly, and everything on the floor will move. Its reading is called t.
Lay down an arrow of length one.
Add a second, shorter arrow, then a third, shorter still. Zeno would halve each step. Our rule is gentler: one over the square root of the step number.
One. Point seven one. Point five eight. Point five. The arrows shrink, but only slowly.
Zeno's halves add up to two and stop. Ours never stop. Sixty arrows reach fourteen, a million reach two thousand. The chain runs off the floor forever.
Now turn the dial. At every joint, bend the chain by the dial reading times the log of the step number. The straight chain curls into a spiral.
The chain is endless, so we add one orange arrow that stands in for the whole rest of the chain. Now the tip is exact.
lines.footnote: the orange arrow is the Euler–Maclaurin tail: N^(1−s)/(s−1) + N^−s/2 + Bernoulli terms

lines.text: Here is the strange talent of the one half rule. Keep turning, and the tip wanders, then dives straight into the centre.
At a dial reading of fourteen point one three, it hits dead centre. We drop a marker on the pole at that height.

chapters.title: Collisions
chapters.subtitle: The tip keeps finding the centre

lines.text: Keep turning. Twenty one. Twenty five. Thirty point four. The tip keeps finding the centre.
It never stops. Riemann proved the collisions go on forever. Ten thousand of them are loaded here, every one on this pole.
Here is the tip's whole path, winding up the pole and threading the centre again and again. Those collision heights are the famous zeros of the zeta function.

chapters.title: Collisions Become Waves
chapters.subtitle: A probability map of the primes

lines.text: Now take the first collision height, fourteen point one three, and turn it into a wave: the cosine of fourteen point one three times the log of x.
Add the wave from the second collision.
And the third.
Ten waves. Most of the time they cancel each other out.
All of them. Where they agree, they pile up into spikes, and the spikes sit exactly on two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen, and their powers: four, eight, nine.
This is a probability map of the primes, built from nothing but collision heights.
Riemann's exact recipe turns the map into a count. Start from the straight line y equals x, and subtract one weighted wave per collision.
Each weight is fixed by the recipe. Nothing is tuned by hand.
lines.footnote: ψ(x) = x − ln 2π − ½ ln(1 − x^-2) − 4√x Σ (cos(γ log x) + 2γ sin(γ log x)) / (1 + 4γ²)

lines.text: The result is a staircase. Every step is a prime: two, three, five, seven, eleven, thirteen. The red markers find them on their own.
More collisions, sharper steps. With a few hundred of them the staircase counts the primes exactly.
Everything so far used the one half rule. Let us move it. Shrink the arrows faster: n to the zero point nine.
Turn the dial. The spiral is tighter, and the tip never hits the centre. No collisions, no markers.
And if we pretend the collisions did happen at zero point nine, every wave grows like x to the zero point nine. The staircase wobbles out of control and stops counting.
lines.footnote: red: the staircase if every collision had shrink rate 0.9 instead of ½

lines.text: The Riemann Hypothesis is the claim that the one half rule is the only one that works: every collision, forever, at exactly one half.
In October 2026, OpenAI published an AI generated proof that no collision can happen with a shrink rate above seven eighths. They call it the quasi Riemann hypothesis.
lines.footnote: openai/math, family 003 · manuscript Sept 30, 2026 · released Oct 6, 2026

lines.text: By symmetry, none below one eighth either. The blue bands are now off limits.
The core theorem is machine checked in Lean, and a companion proof reaches eleven twelfths. Human peer review is still under way, so call it a strong claim, not settled fact.
lines.footnote: Lean: riemannZeta s ≠ 0 for 7/8 < Re s · independently re-checked · not yet peer reviewed

lines.text: The orange gap, from one half to seven eighths, is where the Riemann Hypothesis still lives. Close it, and the primes are finally tamed.
A chain that shrinks by one half. A dial that turns. A tip that keeps striking the centre. And a staircase of primes that falls out of it.
Watch the spiral climb.
